impacts.caseName: Insulet Corp. v. EOFlow, Co. Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the three-year statute of limitations under the Defend Trade Secrets Act (DTSA) barred Insulet's trade secret misappropriation claim when Insulet knew of the alleged misappropriation more than three years before filing suit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed a jury verdict and damages award in favor of Insulet, holding that the DTSA statute of limitations had expired before Insulet filed suit. The court concluded that EOFlow was entitled to judgment as a matter of law because Insulet knew or should have known of the misappropriation more than three years prior to bringing the action. This decision reinforces the strict application of the DTSA's limitations period.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of trade secret misappropriation gain a strong defense where the plaintiff delayed filing suit, as courts will rigorously enforce the three-year DTSA limitations period.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret owners must act promptly upon discovering or having reason to discover misappropriation; delay in filing beyond three years will bar DTSA claims regardless of the strength of the underlying evidence.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly excluded trade secret damages testimony and whether the court erred in its judgment on breach of contract damages arising from software misappropriation.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two previously rejected damages models. The court reversed the breach of contract damages judgment and reinstated the jury award, while affirming Ford's liability for trade secret misappropriation under both the DTSA and Michigan law. This case provides significant guidance on permissible damages methodologies in trade secret litigation.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies asserting trade secret claims benefit from the court's instruction that district courts must give fair consideration to multiple damages theories, including those previously excluded.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies found liable for trade secret misappropriation face potential exposure to broader damages models on remand, and the affirmance of liability confirms the risks of developing competing products while licensing a counterpart's software.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a trial court must defer to the terms of an existing license agreement to assess copyright infringement damages, and whether the court's use of the 'book of wisdom' doctrine and non-compensatory damages was legally permissible.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that courts need not defer to actual license agreement terms when assessing copyright infringement damages via a hypothetical negotiation. However, the court vacated the damages award in part because the trial court adopted a legally impermissible view of the 'book of wisdom' and assessed non-compensatory damages against the government. This case clarifies the framework for computing copyright damages in government software infringement cases.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software companies and copyright holders benefit from the holding that hypothetical negotiation damages are not capped by actual license rates, potentially allowing for higher damages awards.
impacts.negativeImplications: Copyright holders must ensure damages theories are strictly compensatory; courts will reject damages models that include non-compensatory elements or improperly apply hindsight through the book of wisdom doctrine.

impacts.caseName: Ollnova Technologies Ltd. v. ecobee Technologies ULC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a jury verdict form that asks a single infringement question covering multiple patents is reversible error, and whether the district court erred in its § 101 analysis and denial of JMOL on non-infringement.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the $11.5 million infringement and damages judgments and remanded for a new trial, holding that the verdict form's single question covering infringement across all asserted patents was improper. The court also vacated and remanded for further proceedings on patent eligibility under § 101 for the '495 patent while affirming that the '887 and '371 patents were not directed to abstract ideas. This decision reinforces the requirement for patent-specific verdict forms in multi-patent cases.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the requirement that verdict forms must separately address each asserted patent, preventing ambiguous verdicts that obscure which patents are actually infringed.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face increased procedural complexity and risk of new trials if verdict forms do not separately identify infringement findings for each asserted patent.

impacts.caseName: Ironburg Inventions Ltd. v. Valve Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly applied inter partes review estoppel under 35 U.S.C. § 315(e)(2) to bar Valve from asserting invalidity grounds that were not included in its original IPR petition.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's application of IPR estoppel against two of Valve's invalidity grounds. The court found that the district court relied on insufficient evidence to estop one ground and failed to adequately account for hindsight bias in estopping the other. This decision narrows the scope of IPR estoppel and provides important guidance on the 'reasonably could have raised' standard.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from a more rigorous standard for IPR estoppel, preserving their ability to raise invalidity defenses in district court that were not included in IPR petitions, particularly where the prior art was not reasonably discoverable.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face greater difficulty in using IPR estoppel to foreclose invalidity defenses in litigation, potentially increasing the cost and complexity of patent enforcement.

impacts.caseName: Enanta Pharmaceuticals, Inc. v. Pfizer Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a change from 'C2-C12-alkyl' to 'C1-C12-alkyl' between a provisional application and a non-provisional application constituted an obvious typographical error correctable without adding new matter, thus preserving the earlier priority date.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity, holding that the alteration in the chemical formula between Enanta's provisional and non-provisional applications was not an obvious typographical error and therefore introduced new matter. Because the non-provisional could not claim priority from the provisional, Pfizer's intervening public disclosure of nirmatrelvir anticipated the patent claims. This decision has major implications for pharmaceutical patent strategy and provisional application drafting.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic drug manufacturers and competitors benefit from strict enforcement of priority requirements, as errors in provisional applications may invalidate later-filed patents covering blockbuster drugs.
impacts.negativeImplications: Pharmaceutical companies and patent applicants face heightened risk from drafting errors in provisional applications; even minor typographical errors may be deemed new matter, destroying priority and exposing claims to intervening prior art.

impacts.caseName: Board of Regents of the University of Texas System v. Boston Scientific Corp.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Boston Scientific was entitled to judgment as a matter of law of invalidity for anticipation and non-infringement of claims directed to drug-releasing biodegradable fiber implants used in coronary stents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the jury's infringement verdict in favor of the University of Texas, holding that Boston Scientific was entitled to JMOL of both invalidity for anticipation and non-infringement. The court found the prior art fully anticipated the asserted claims covering drug-eluting stent technology. This decision eliminates potential damages exposure for BSC's coronary stent product line.
impacts.positiveImplications: Medical device companies benefit from the court's rigorous application of anticipation analysis, providing a strong defense against overbroad claims on drug-eluting stent technology.
impacts.negativeImplications: University patent holders and licensors face increased difficulty enforcing broad composition claims when prior art references disclose the essential elements, even after obtaining favorable jury verdicts.

impacts.caseName: AGI SureTrack LLC v. Farmers Edge Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether claims directed to automated systems for capturing, processing, and sharing farming data using GPS-equipped relay devices attached to farming equipment are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that AGI's asserted patent claims directed to farming data collection and sharing are patent-ineligible abstract ideas under § 101, while vacating and remanding the district court's determination that the case was not exceptional for potential attorney fee award. The decision extends the reach of § 101 invalidity to agricultural technology patents claiming data collection and processing methods.
impacts.positiveImplications: Agricultural technology companies and accused infringers benefit from the affirmance that farming data collection and processing claims may be patent-ineligible, reducing exposure to infringement suits involving abstract data management concepts.
impacts.negativeImplications: AgTech patent holders face significant risk that claims framed around data capture, processing, and sharing—even using specific hardware like relay devices—will be found patent-ineligible, and the remand on exceptionality raises the specter of fee-shifting.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the six-year statute of limitations under 28 U.S.C. § 2501 for claims in the Court of Federal Claims is subject to American Pipe class action tolling.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that 28 U.S.C. § 2501's six-year statute of limitations is not subject to American Pipe tolling, affirming dismissal of breach of contract and takings claims by bank holding companies that lost assets during the 2008 financial crisis. The court recognized that its prior decision in Bright v. United States was implicitly overruled by the Supreme Court's decision in ANZ Securities. This ruling has broad implications for class action members with claims in the Court of Federal Claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: The government and defendants in Court of Federal Claims litigation benefit from certainty that § 2501's limitations period runs regardless of pending class actions, reducing the risk of stale claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Businesses and individuals with claims against the government must independently file within the six-year limitations period and cannot rely on the pendency of a class action to toll the statute, potentially resulting in forfeiture of meritorious claims.

impacts.caseName: Otsuka America Pharmaceutical, Inc. v. Hetero Labs Limited
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly construed the claim terms 'dextromethorphan' and 'quinidine' in the weight-to-weight ratio limitation, and whether the court permissibly waived the Rule 65(c) bond requirement pending appeal of a preliminary injunction.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the preliminary injunction blocking Hetero's generic drug from competing with Otsuka's Nuedexta but vacated the district court's waiver of the Rule 65(c) bond requirement pending appeal. The court upheld the claim construction but held that equitable considerations alone are insufficient to waive the bond, requiring the enjoined party to have security against wrongful injunction damages. This decision is significant for pharmaceutical patent litigation and preliminary injunction practice.
impacts.positiveImplications: Branded pharmaceutical companies benefit from the affirmance of the preliminary injunction, maintaining market exclusivity for Nuedexta during litigation. The claim construction holding supports broad interpretation of drug compound terms.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic drug companies benefit from the bond requirement reinstatement, ensuring they have recourse if a preliminary injunction is later found wrongful. Patent holders seeking preliminary injunctions must post bonds, increasing the cost of enforcement.

impacts.caseName: mCom IP, LLC v. City National Bank of Florida
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may dismiss a patent infringement complaint on the pleadings based on obviousness grounds from a prior IPR against different claims of the same patent, and whether the grounds presented supported an exceptional case finding under § 285 or attorney sanctions under § 1927.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed dismissal of a patent infringement complaint where the asserted claims were found invalid on the same obviousness grounds that the PTAB applied to other claims of the same patent in an IPR. However, the court reversed the § 285 exceptional case fee award and § 1927 attorney sanctions, finding the grounds insufficient to establish that the case was exceptional or that counsel acted in bad faith. This decision calibrates the standards for fee-shifting in patent cases.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders and their attorneys benefit from the reversal of sanctions and fee awards, establishing that pursuing surviving patent claims—even when related claims were invalidated in IPR—does not automatically constitute bad faith or exceptional conduct.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies defending against patent infringement may face continued suits on surviving claims even after successful IPR proceedings, though they retain the ability to seek dismissal on the same invalidity theories applied to related claims.

impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner that grants an exclusive license but retains the right to sue third parties for infringement and other exclusionary rights has sufficient constitutional standing to bring a patent infringement suit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal for lack of standing, holding that a patent owner retains constitutional standing to sue for infringement when it reserves the right to sue third parties and other exclusionary rights, even after granting an exclusive license. The court found the retained right to sue was not rendered illusory by the license terms. This decision clarifies standing requirements for patent owners who have granted exclusive licenses.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners who license their patents exclusively can preserve standing to enforce patents by retaining the right to sue for infringement and other meaningful exclusionary rights in the license agreement.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers cannot easily challenge standing based on the existence of an exclusive license when the patent owner has retained substantive enforcement rights.

impacts.caseName: TrackTime, LLC v. Amazon.com Services LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether claim terms reciting 'executable program code configured to' perform specified functions should be construed as means-plus-function terms under 35 U.S.C. § 112(f) in light of the Federal Circuit's intervening precedent in Dyfan v. Target Corp.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the district court's indefiniteness ruling on the '978 patent and remanded for reconsideration of whether § 112(f) applies, in light of the court's intervening precedent in Dyfan v. Target Corp. The court affirmed the invalidity judgment on the '638 patent claim for anticipation. This decision provides important guidance on when software-related claim terms trigger means-plus-function treatment.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software patent holders benefit from the opportunity to argue that 'executable program code' claim terms are not means-plus-function limitations, potentially avoiding indefiniteness invalidity.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies accused of software patent infringement face uncertainty as courts reconsider whether common software claim formulations invoke § 112(f), potentially broadening claim scope.

impacts.caseName: Actelion Pharmaceuticals Ltd v. Mylan Pharmaceuticals Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the claim term 'a pH of 13 or higher' in pharmaceutical composition patents should be measured at a standard temperature in the field, and whether the patentee was barred from asserting infringement under the doctrine of equivalents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed non-infringement of Actelion's epoprostenol formulation patents, holding that the claim term 'a pH of 13 or higher' refers to pH measured at a temperature standard in the field. The court also upheld the district court's ruling that Actelion was barred from asserting infringement by equivalents. This decision has practical significance for pharmaceutical patent claims involving pH-dependent formulations.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic drug manufacturers benefit from precise claim construction of measurable parameters, reducing uncertainty about whether their formulations infringe composition-of-matter patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Pharmaceutical patent holders must draft claims with precision regarding measurement conditions; failure to specify temperature standards for pH claims may narrow the scope of patent protection.

impacts.caseName: Wyeth LLC v. AstraZeneca Pharmaceuticals LP
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether broad patent claims directed to methods of treating EGFR-resistant non-small cell lung cancer with irreversible EGFR inhibitors are invalid as a matter of law for lack of enablement or other grounds.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed JMOL of invalidity of Wyeth's cancer treatment method patents, which claimed use of irreversible EGFR inhibitors to treat gefitinib/erlotinib-resistant NSCLC. The court found the claims invalid despite the jury having found in Wyeth's favor at trial. This decision underscores the stringent requirements for broad method-of-treatment claims in pharmaceutical patents, particularly where the specification discloses only limited examples.
impacts.positiveImplications: Pharmaceutical competitors benefit from the invalidation of broad treatment method claims, clearing the path for development and marketing of irreversible EGFR inhibitor cancer drugs without infringement risk.
impacts.negativeImplications: Innovator pharmaceutical companies face heightened invalidity risk for broad method-of-treatment claims supported by only a few disclosed compounds, even after obtaining favorable jury verdicts.
